schools.summary: Gill defends the right of a man whose character is attacked to answer, and is particular about the physics of sea sand.
Henry draws the rule that a discourse must be heard out, and reads the swallowed words as an apology offered in advance.
Clarke makes the sand both uncountable and unweighable, and turns the weighing into a demand for justice.
Ellicott hears a man baulked of sympathy from whom no formal argument should be expected; Keil and Delitzsch set the two scales and gloss the noun for calamity.
Gregory the Great makes the friends' talk part of the trial, sorer than the scourges, and weighs Job's few excessive words against the Judge's own verdict on him.

debates.question: How should Job's reply to Eliphaz be judged?

sides.position: Passion growing more violent for being checked; words recorded for admonition, not imitation
A man who gave thanks under the scourges and answered rightly when galled with words
Not an argument at all, but the reiterated complaint of a man denied sympathy

outliers.note: The only patristic voice in the chapter, and the only one who treats the friends' speeches as a distinct temptation permitted for Job's trial.

1.pericope_label: Oh that my grief were throughly weighed; heavier than the sand of the sea

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the outward strokes called God's arrows from the inward distress the verse really means.
Clarke describes a poisoned wound and quotes an Eastern saying about God as the unerring archer; Wesley makes the poison the wrath the arrows were dipped in.
Ellicott corrects the English on the drinking up of the spirit and keeps the military sense of the terrors in array.

debates.question: What do the arrows of the Almighty stand for?

sides.position: Chiefly the inward distress, with a keen sense of the divine displeasure behind the outward strokes
Literal poisoned shafts, with the fever and mania such wounds produce
Afflictions dipped in wrath, which burn up the vital parts as well as pierce

outliers.note: Alone in quoting the Eastern parable of heaven as a bow and God as the unerring archer, and in preferring Mr. Good's rendering of the insipid food.

themes: the wild ass and the ox
4.pericope_label: The arrows of the Almighty are within me; doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass?

schools.summary: Gill works the senses of the petition and insists the destruction asked for is of the body only.
Henry calls the request ill said, marks the limit the sufferer kept, and refuses to follow him in hardening.
Clarke takes the hardening for resolution rather than defiance and reports a variant reading of the comfort clause.
Ellicott calls the hope one from God rather than in God, and finds the sequence of thought obscure.

debates.question: How is the wish to be destroyed to be taken?

sides.position: As passion, ill said and recorded for our admonition, though it stopped short of self-murder
As the common error of sufferers who look for relief in changed circumstances rather than in themselves
As the reasonable request of a man with no hope of being redeemed from a helpless state

outliers.note: Alone in listing the renderings of the hardening clause, a phrase occurring nowhere else in scripture.

themes: that God would grant my request
I have not concealed his words
8.pericope_label: Oh that I might have my request, and that God would grant me the thing I long for

schools.summary: Gill reads the question about help as a claim of self-defence backed by a good conscience.
Clarke brings Cicero and Homer for the proverb about flesh and stone, and denies any sign of a deranged mind in the chapter.
Keil and Delitzsch gloss the idiom of drawing out the soul as forbearance; Ellicott offers two constructions of the last question and chooses neither.

debates.question: What does the question about help in him mean?

sides.position: A claim: it is in his power to defend himself, with conscience and argument on his side
A confession that his help is all in himself and therefore perfect weakness — but not that reason is gone
Either a bare statement that wisdom is driven from him, or a complaint that the friends are driving it

outliers.note: Alone in arguing that nothing in the chapter marks a mind deranged or even impaired.

11.pericope_label: What is my strength, that I should hope? Is my flesh of brass?

schools.summary: Gill catalogues the afflictions that make pity a debt and stresses that these were brethren by religion among idolaters.
Henry makes compassion a debt and inhumanity irreligion, and works the brook through its three stages.
Clarke prefers a variant that shames the despiser of his friend, and brings a classical adage and a Latin satire against him.
Ellicott vouches for the simile from his own travel; Keil and Delitzsch reject an interpolation that Hitzig called a swindle.

debates.question: Who is it that forsakes the fear of the Almighty in this verse?

sides.position: The friend who withholds compassion, as the Latin and the Chaldee make it
The sufferer, who may be driven to forsake it if gentleness is denied him
Uncertain: the clause admits three constructions and the English version is not one of them

outliers.note: Alone in reporting the thirty-two manuscripts that turn the reproach upon the man who despises his friend.

14.pericope_label: To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed; my brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook

schools.summary: Gill allows the blackness two applications and prefers the one that makes it the friends' own hearts.
Clarke keeps to the physics of freezing and evaporation; Wesley marks the seasons and the scarcity of water in Arabia.
Ellicott finds the clause ambiguous between streams and travellers; Keil and Delitzsch render the caravans' shame.

debates.question: Does the clause about paths turned aside describe the streams or the caravans?

sides.position: The caravans, which turn aside into the waste and perish, as the next verse suggests
The streams, which divide into lesser channels and are lost in the sand

outliers.note: Alone in vouching for the simile from his own travel, having seen the great river at Cordova reduced in August to a third-rate stream.

themes: blackish by reason of the ice
16.pericope_label: The troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them

schools.summary: Gill weighs the written text against the margin and commends Mr. Broughton for keeping both.
Henry makes the restraint a virtue and the neglect worse for it, since all that was wanted was a good look and a good word.
Clarke matches the friends to the deceitful torrents exactly; Wesley reads their fear as fear for themselves.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both prefer the reading that makes them become nothing, as the Targum takes it.

debates.question: What does the clause now ye are nothing read?

sides.position: Ye are become like it, that is, like the brook just described
Ye are become nothing, as though ye had never been
Ye are to me as if you had never come, for I have no comfort from you

outliers.note: Alone in drawing the comparison that from men, even when we expect little, we have less, while from God, even when we expect much, we have more.

themes: did I say, Bring unto me
a good look and a good word
20.pericope_label: Ye see my casting down, and are afraid; did I say, Bring unto me?

schools.summary: Gill turns the offer to be taught into a character of good men who will learn even from inferiors.
Clarke finds the friends' premises false and their conclusions empty, and reports a variant reading of forcible; Wesley denies their arguments any weight.
Keil and Delitzsch canvass Hupfeld's and Hahn's renderings of the disputed word and reject both; Ellicott prefers open rebuke to secret love.

debates.question: What is the disputed word in the praise of right words?

sides.position: Forcible, the common reading, which Clarke prefers though a variant gives savoury
Not the sweeter sense, which suits this verse but not a later one, nor Hupfeld's bitter, nor Hahn's bad

outliers.note: Alone in reading the couplet as a preference for honest open rebuke over insinuations meant to pass for friendship.

themes: teach me and I will hold my tongue
the speech of one in despair
24.pericope_label: Teach me, and I will hold my tongue; how forcible are right words

schools.summary: Gill lists what the Jewish commentators make fall upon the fatherless, and limits the question about the tongue to the words actually charged.
Clarke reads the two halves as one accusation and closes with an account of his own labour on the chapter.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch prefer the harder rendering about casting lots and trafficking, and Ellicott reflects on the difficulty of tracing the argument.

debates.question: How should the charge about the fatherless be rendered?

sides.position: Ye overwhelm the fatherless and dig a pit for your friend
Ye would cast lots upon the fatherless and make merchandise of your friend, which keeps the parallelism

outliers.note: Alone in stepping outside the text to describe his own editorial labour, and in judging that the chapter might have ended the controversy.

27.pericope_label: Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity; is there iniquity in my tongue?
